# Árgos walks into a cybersecurity & digital protection firm

Somewhere right now, in a cybersecurity & digital protection office, someone is doing exactly what the myths describe — and has never heard of **Árgos**. This file is the introduction.

## Before the Office, the Story

**Hera Sets the Watch.** Zeús loved Io, daughter of the river-god Inachos, and to hide her from Hera — so the common telling runs — she was changed into a white cow.  Hera was not deceived.  She asked for the cow as a gift, and set over it Árgos Panoptes, the all-seeing giant, who tethered his prisoner to an olive tree in the grove of Mycenae and watched her without rest.

**The Herdsman Who Never Sleeps.** Árgos kept Io as a cowherd keeps a beast: by day she grazed under his eyes, by night she was bound.  The poets dwell on the horror of it — a princess eating grass, a guard with nowhere to look away.  Aeschylus makes him the many-eyed herdsman whose vigil not even the earth could bury.

## Not the First Rebrand

Árgos never became a god and was never identified with foreign deities; his afterlife is in the natural world and in language.  Rome kept him as Argus — Ovid's account in the Metamorphoses is the fullest surviving version — and made the transfer of his eyes the aition, the explanatory myth, of the peacock's plumage. The office is only the latest translation.
